rationale: The literature on engagement is fragmented: engagement falls steeply over months (c1), is measured in 23 different ways (c2), fails for reasons that include the absence of clinician response (c3), and is limited by access (c4). A scoping review maps definitions, duration, features, support, outcomes and non-engagement without pretending to pool incompatible measures. JBI guidance with PRISMA-ScR reporting.
alternatives: Systematic review of engagement and seizure outcomes (refused: engagement definitions are incompatible and no trial links engagement to seizures)
Clinic questionnaire of app users (refused for now: the review must not involve clinic patients)
Decide on coaching without evidence (refused: the clinic asked for a map first)
whyNotMoreComplex: Pooling needs comparable measures, which do not exist; a map answers what the clinic needs before July.

decision.statement: Run a scoping review of engagement with epilepsy self-management apps, charting definitions and measures, levels and duration, features and clinician support, outcomes reported with engagement, and who does not engage, to inform the July 2027 clinic decision.
decision.question: Should the clinic map the evidence on app engagement before choosing between nurse coaching and a hospital-built app?

criteria.text: Engagement evidence is fragmented, short and measured inconsistently, so a map is the useful product.
A current scoping review of epilepsy app engagement already answers these questions.

gates.evidence: Library request NSL-2026-118 dated 2026-09-03, supplied by the investigator

gates.evidence: Department memo NEU-2026-22: three hours a week each, October 2026 to June 2027, supplied by the investigator

alternatives: Systematic review of engagement and seizure outcomes
Decide on coaching without a review
